title: James Knox
summary: Before Boone's fame, long hunter Col. James Knox led Virginia and Carolina hunters through Cumberland Gap into Kentucky on a long hunt.
bodyMarkdown:
Years before Boone's name filled the histories, [Col. James Knox](/people/#james-knox) was already deep in the Kentucky country. Knox was a western Virginia hunter, and in 1769 he led a large party from southwest Virginia and North Carolina through Cumberland Gap to hunt and trap. The [ExploreKYHistory entry for marker #709](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/1000) counts about forty men.

They came with horses, rifles, and camp gear, and they meant to stay a long time. That is where the name came from. Hunters who stayed out for many months, sometimes years, came home as the [Long Hunters](https://grokipedia.com/page/Longhunter).

Knox's men worked the country of the upper Green River and the Barrens. An 1892 biography says a friendly Cherokee leader, [Captain Dick](/people/#captain-dick), pointed a small party toward richer game in the Bluegrass. The stream they found there is still called Dix River, after "Dick's."

In what is now Green County, Knox and his men built a camp and a skin house. The 1942 Historic Camp Knox marker says twenty-two men cured and stored some 2,300 deer hides there, and Green County's history says the hunters named the nearby branch Skinhouse Branch.

The dates are not settled. The markers put the Green County camp in 1770–1771. The 1892 biography puts it in 1774. Other accounts place Knox with [Kasper Mansker](/people/#kasper-mansker), [Joseph Drake](/people/#joseph-drake), and [Henry Skaggs](/people/#henry-skaggs) in 1769, when that party is said to have come upon [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone) singing on a deerskin.

The same 1892 biography says neither party knew the other was there. This story follows the markers.

The Revolution pulled Knox east. He raised a company for the 8th Virginia Regiment and commanded a company at the Battle of Saratoga. After the war he came back to Kentucky and went into public life. He served in the Virginia legislature in 1788 and in the Kentucky Senate from Lincoln County from 1795 to 1800.

In 1805 Knox married Ann Montgomery Logan, the widow of [Benjamin Logan](/stories/benjamin-logan/). He died in 1822. His fellow long hunter [Henry Skaggs](/stories/henry-skaggs-green-river-long-hunter/) worked the same Green River country.

## Kentucky today

The Historic Camp Knox marker stands in Green County, near the skin-house camp. State historical marker #709, "Benj. Logan — Pioneer," at Taylorsville Road and Brunerstown Road in Shelbyville, honors both Logan and Knox.
